To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

metabolic channel" is an inappropriate term to describe the effect of scaffolds, and that scaffolds are only useful in systems with sequestration reactions or in large cells, where the characteristic time of substrate transfer is longer than the time required for the substrate to diffuse away from the scaffold.

the concept of "metabolite channeling" as an increase in the direct transfer of freely diffusable intermediate molecules between enzymes due to their proximity on a scaffold is only beneficial in the initial phase of the reaction and in systems with sequestration of intermediate molecules".

the benefit of placing enzyme pairs on scaffolding in a confined container depends on: the lifetime of substrate molecules, the lifetime of enzyme pairs on the scaffold, and the lifetime of enzyme molecules in the container.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of enzyme cascades on nanostructured scaffolds and with the analysis of the resulting reaction kinetics and product distribution.
the origins of the observed activity enhancement of enzyme cascades on nanoscale scaffold.
the origins of activity enhancement in multienzyme systems and with the development of new strategies for the design of enzyme cascades on nanoscale surfaces.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
scaffolds can be beneficial in some cases, but the conditions under which this is true are not well defined.
the concept of "metabolite channeling" is a myth.

scaffolds are beneficial for enzyme cascades if the substrate molecules are not free to move, if the substrate molecules have a short lifetime in the container or if the substrate molecules interact weakly with the scaffold.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
metabolic channelizing" is a useful concept for describing the initial boost to cascade throughput due to the proximity and orientation of enzymes on scaffolds.
the use of scaffolds is not always beneficial, and the benefit is not always due to "metabolic channelization" or substrate diffusion.
the use of scaffolds to enhance cascade activity in small cells is not justified by the results of this study.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the concept of "metabolite channeling" is only relevant for the initial stages of the cascade, when the product molecules of one enzyme are still scarce.
a scaffold can be beneficial in a variety of systems, but only if the substrate is confined in the container.
enzyme cascades can be boosted by placing individual enzyme pairs onto a scaffold only if substrate molecules are sequestered.
